boss.caption1: The late-night text from your boss.
boss.incoming: Can we talk first thing tomorrow? We need to go over the Henderson report.
boss.bad: If this is about the deadline, I told you weeks ago it wasn't realistic. Not my fault.
boss.question: My boss wants to talk about a report that went badly. I'm anxious and defensive. How do I reply?
boss.answerLead: Lead with openness, not a defense.
boss.answerTry: Try: “Sure, 9 works. I'd like to walk through what happened and how we fix it.”
boss.good: Sure, 9 works. I'd like to walk through what happened and how we fix it.
narration: [anxious] A late text from your boss. Your stomach drops, and the defense writes itself.
[regretful, slower] But you know how that would sound in the morning.
[calm, warm] So you pause. You tell Tack you're anxious, not guilty. And it helps you answer like the professional you are.
[relieved] Calm. Open. Ready to fix it. And the meeting starts on your side.
[warm, steady] Stay anchored. Find direction. The Anchored Compass.

partner.incoming: Totally forgot we had dinner plans tonight 😬 Work ran late. Rain check?
partner.bad: Of course you forgot. I'm always last on your list.
partner.question: My partner forgot our dinner plans again. I feel unimportant. How do I say that without a fight?
partner.answerLead: Share the impact, not the verdict.
partner.answerTry: Try: “I was really looking forward to tonight. When plans slip, I feel less important. Can we talk about it?”
partner.good: I was really looking forward to tonight. When plans slip, I feel less important. Can we talk about it?
partner.reply: You're right. I'm sorry. Let's talk when I get home 💛
narration: [hurt] They forgot. Again. And it stings more than you want to admit.
[regretful, slower] The words are sharp... and you know they'd cut both ways.
[calm, warm] So you pause. You tell Tack what it really feels like: unimportant. And it helps you say it plainly.
[relieved] Honest. Not cruel. And this time, they actually hear you.
[warm, steady] Stay anchored. Find direction. The Anchored Compass.

coparent.incoming: Can't do pickup Friday. You'll need to get the kids.
coparent.bad: Unbelievable. You never stick to the schedule and I always have to fix it.
coparent.question: My co-parent canceled pickup last minute again. I'm furious. How do I keep it about the kids?
coparent.answerLead: Stick to the plan, not the past.
coparent.answerTry: Try: “I can get them Friday at 5. Going forward, can we confirm pickups by Wednesday?”
coparent.good: I can get them Friday at 5. Going forward, can we confirm pickups by Wednesday?
coparent.reply: That works. I'll confirm by Wednesday. Thanks.
narration: [exasperated] Another last-minute change. And every old fight comes rushing back.
[regretful, slower] But this isn't about winning. It's about the kids.
[calm, warm] So you pause. You tell Tack you're furious, and tired. And it helps you keep it simple, and about them.
[relieved] A plan, not a fight. And Friday just got easier.
[warm, steady] Stay anchored. Find direction. The Anchored Compass.

coworker.incoming: Great meeting today! Glad the client liked my idea 🙌
coworker.bad: YOUR idea? That was my proposal and you know it.
coworker.question: A coworker took credit for my work in front of a client. How do I address it without starting a war?
coworker.answerTry: Try: “Can we grab 10 minutes tomorrow? I want to talk about how we share credit on the proposal.”
coworker.good: Can we grab 10 minutes tomorrow? I want to talk about how we share credit on the proposal.
coworker.reply: Sure, 10 a.m.? And you're right, I should have named you.
narration: [angry] Your work. Their name. And the anger is instant.
[regretful, slower] But a callout in writing lasts forever.
[calm, warm] So you pause. You tell Tack what happened, and how it felt. And it helps you ask for a real conversation.
[confident, warm] Direct. Private. Fair. And your work gets the credit it deserves.
[warm, steady] Stay anchored. Find direction. The Anchored Compass.

mom.incoming: So when are you coming home? It's been months. Your sister visits every weekend.
mom.bad: Maybe if every visit wasn't a guilt trip, I'd come more.
mom.question: My mom keeps guilt-tripping me about visiting. I love her, but I feel pressured. How do I set a kind boundary?
mom.answerLead: Lead with love, then the limit.
mom.answerTry: Try: “I love you and I miss you too. I can't come this month, but let's plan a weekend in December.”
mom.good: I love you and I miss you too. I can't come this month, but let's plan a weekend in December.
mom.reply: That would make me so happy. December it is ❤️
narration: [frustrated, tender] The same question. The same guilt. And all of it comes out at once.
[regretful, slower] But she's still your mom... and that's not what you mean.
[calm, warm] So you pause. You tell Tack you love her, and you feel pressured. And it helps you say both.
[warm, relieved] Love first. Then the limit. And it lands softly.
[warm, steady] Stay anchored. Find direction. The Anchored Compass.

day29_holiday.caption1: The question you know is coming.
day29_holiday.incoming: See you at Thanksgiving! Hope you're finally bringing someone this year 😉
day29_holiday.bad: Maybe I would if this family didn't interrogate everyone I date.
day29_holiday.question: My aunt asks about my love life every Thanksgiving. I'm already dreading it. What do I say?
day29_holiday.answerLead: Decide it now, while you're calm.
day29_holiday.answerTry: Try: “Just me this year! Can't wait to hear about your trip.”
day29_holiday.good: Just me this year! Can't wait to see you and hear all about your trip.
day29_holiday.reply: Oh, I have SO many pictures! See you Thursday ❤️
narration: [dread] The holidays are coming. And so is the question you know they'll ask.
[regretful, slower] But a sharp answer now just sets the table for a fight.
[calm, warm] So you pause. You tell Tack you're dreading it. And it helps you plan a short, kind answer, while you're calm.
[relieved] Short. Kind. New topic. You don't owe anyone a debate over dinner.
[warm, steady] Stay anchored. Find direction. The Anchored Compass.

day30_hardtext.caption1: Your thumbs are faster than you.
day30_hardtext.incoming: Did you take my charger again? That's the third time this week.
day30_hardtext.bad: Wow. Maybe keep track of your own stuff before you accuse me.
day30_hardtext.question: My roommate just accused me of taking their charger. I want to snap back. Should I?
day30_hardtext.answerLead: Ask what you actually want to happen.
day30_hardtext.answerTry: Try: “I don't think I have it, but I'll help you look. Want a shared charging spot?”
day30_hardtext.good: I don't think I have it, but I'll help you look. Want to set up a shared charging spot?
day30_hardtext.reply: Found it in my bag 🤦 Sorry! And yes, good idea.
narration: [irritated] An accusation lands, and your thumbs are already typing.
[regretful, slower] But would you say that out loud, to their face? Probably not.
[calm, warm] So you pause. Tack asks what you actually want to happen. And it helps you say just that.
[relieved, light] Calm words. And the problem solves itself.
[warm, steady] Stay anchored. Find direction. The Anchored Compass.
